name: Variable
quick: A symbol standing for a value in a stated setting.
definition: A variable is a named placeholder. Its allowed values and its role come from the statement where it occurs; the same letter may have a different meaning in a different problem. Giving a value or quantifying the variable can turn an open numerical condition into a proposition.
example: In $x+3=9$, $x$ is an unspecified number. Substituting $x=6$ produces the true proposition $6+3=9$.
confusion: Do not carry a letter’s meaning into a new example unless the author says it is retained.

name: Propositional variable
quick: A letter standing for a true-or-false statement.
definition: A propositional variable names a proposition so that its logical relationships can be studied without repeating its wording. An assignment supplies its truth value. Unlike a numerical variable, it is combined by logical operators rather than ordinary arithmetic.
example: If $p$ means “the server is online,” then $\neg p$ says “the server is not online.”
confusion: A letter does not have one permanent meaning throughout a course. Read the declarations in each example.

name: Boolean algebra
quick: Algebra of true-or-false values and logical operations.
definition: In the two-valued setting of this course, Boolean algebra studies truth values and operations such as AND, OR, and NOT. Logical identities allow one expression to be replaced by another with the same truth table. The subject is named for George Boole.
example: $p\land T$ has the same truth value as $p$: requiring something already true adds no condition.
confusion: AND and OR have their own laws. Similar-looking rules from numerical algebra cannot be transferred without justification.

name: Truthiness
quick: A programming convention that converts other values to truth values.
definition: Some programming languages allow values such as numbers or strings where a condition is expected and convert them to true or false. The conversion convention depends on the language. Here logical operators act on values already specified as true or false.
example: A language might treat numeric zero as false in a condition. That is a language rule, not the mathematical proposition $0=0$, which is true.
confusion: Never assume that all languages convert values in the same way.

name: Pairwise and triple intersections
quick: Intersections involving two sets at a time, or three together.
definition: For three sets, the pairwise intersections are obtained by choosing two of the sets at a time. The triple intersection consists of elements belonging to all three. An element in the triple intersection belongs to every pairwise intersection as well.
example: For $A=\{1,2\}$, $B=\{2,3\}$, $C=\{2,4\}$, all three pairwise intersections and the triple intersection are $\{2\}$.
confusion: A pairwise intersection does not exclude elements also belonging to a third set.

name: Length of a walk
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs
quick: The number of connections traversed, counting repetitions.
definition: A walk is a sequence of vertices in which consecutive vertices are joined in the permitted direction. Its length is the number of traversed edges, including any repeated traversals. A walk consisting of one vertex has length zero.
example: The walk $a,b,c$ uses two connections and has length 2, although three vertices are written.
confusion: In an unweighted graph, length counts edges. It is not the physical length of the drawn lines.

name: Reachability
quick: Whether one object can be reached by following permitted connections.
definition: A vertex is reachable from another when a walk following the permitted edge directions leads from the starting vertex to it. One must state whether zero-length walks are allowed: these make every vertex reachable from itself.
example: If the connections are $a\to b$ and $b\to c$, then $c$ is reachable from $a$. The converse need not hold.
confusion: A relation’s transitive closure describes positive-length walks; its reflexive-transitive closure also includes zero-length walks.

name: Block in a counting argument
quick: Several adjacent objects temporarily treated as one unit.
definition: When specified objects must be consecutive in an arrangement, group them as a block, arrange that unit with the remaining objects, and count permitted internal orders. The method is valid when each final arrangement has exactly one such description.
example: Arrange A, B, C, D with A next to B. There are $3!$ arrangements of the units (AB), C, D and two internal orders, giving $2\cdot3!=12$.
confusion: This “block” is an adjacent unit in a counting model. A block of a set partition need not have any notion of adjacency.

name: Endpoint
quick: A vertex at one end of an edge.
definition: An edge joining two vertices has those vertices as its endpoints. In a simple undirected graph the endpoints are distinct and their order does not matter.
example: The edge $\{a,c\}$ has endpoints $a$ and $c$.
confusion: The place where two drawn lines cross is not an endpoint unless a vertex is explicitly placed there.

name: Degree list
quick: The degrees of the vertices, listed in an indicated order.
definition: A degree list records one degree for each vertex. If no vertex order is given, lists are often sorted for comparison; a labeled list must say which vertex each number belongs to. The sum of the degrees of an undirected graph is twice its edge count.
example: For the triangle $a,b,c$ with one additional edge $\{c,d\}$, the list in order $a,b,c,d$ is $2,2,3,1$.
confusion: A list of nonnegative integers is not automatically realizable by a simple graph.

name: Handshaking lemma
quick: Every undirected edge contributes two to the total degree.
definition: In a finite undirected graph each edge has two ends. Counting incident ends vertex by vertex therefore gives twice the number of edges. Under our simple-graph convention there are no loops; in a model with loops, each loop contributes two ends at its vertex.
example: Four edges give total degree 8. The list $2,2,3,1$ has this total.
confusion: An even degree sum is necessary for a degree list, but is not sufficient to realize it as a simple graph.

name: Graph distance
quick: The minimum number of edges in a route between two reachable vertices.
definition: In an unweighted graph, the distance from one vertex to a reachable vertex is the least number of edges in any walk connecting them, respecting directions when present. The distance from a vertex to itself is zero. If no route exists, a finite distance is not defined.
example: In the path $a,b,c$, the distance from $a$ to $c$ is 2.
confusion: Graph distance depends on connections, not on how far apart dots appear in a drawing.

name: Strong connectivity
quick: Every vertex of a nonempty digraph can reach every other.
definition: A directed graph is strongly connected when it is nonempty and for every ordered pair of vertices a directed path connects the first to the second. The direction of each edge must be respected. Our empty-graph convention excludes the empty digraph.
example: A directed three-cycle is strongly connected. A one-way chain $a\to b\to c$ is not.
confusion: Ignoring arrowheads tests weak connectivity, a different property.

name: Weak connectivity
quick: A nonempty digraph becomes connected when directions are ignored.
definition: A digraph is weakly connected when forgetting its arrowheads gives a connected undirected graph. This does not require the directed routes themselves to work in both directions. Our convention excludes the empty digraph.
example: The chain $a\to b\to c$ is weakly connected: after ignoring directions, all three vertices are joined.
confusion: Weak connectivity alone does not allow directed travel from every vertex to every other.

name: Spanning tree
quick: A tree that uses every vertex of a connected graph.
definition: A spanning tree keeps all the vertices of a connected undirected graph and selects enough of its edges to remain connected without any cycle. A graph can have several spanning trees. Removing a cycle edge while preserving connectivity eventually produces one.
example: Removing any one edge from a triangle leaves a spanning tree with all three vertices and two edges.
confusion: A spanning tree may omit edges but cannot omit vertices.

name: Internal vertex of a rooted tree
quick: A rooted-tree vertex with at least one child.
definition: After a root is chosen, every other vertex has a parent on the path toward the root. An internal vertex has one or more children; a leaf has none. These roles depend on the rooted structure.
example: In a root with two leaf children, the root is the only internal vertex.
confusion: “Internal” does not mean geometrically inside the drawing. A root can be a leaf if it has no children.

name: Binary tree
quick: A rooted tree in which each vertex has at most two children.
definition: A binary tree has at most two children per vertex. A full binary tree is the more restricted case in which every internal vertex has exactly two. The number of children is counted away from the chosen root.
example: A chain rooted at one endpoint is a binary tree but is not full when it has an internal vertex with only one child.
confusion: A non-root vertex may have undirected degree three: one parent plus two children.

name: Graph traversal
quick: A systematic process for visiting vertices and examining connections.
definition: A graph traversal follows an algorithm that records which vertices have been encountered and selects which connections to explore next. To cover a disconnected graph, restart from an unvisited vertex after one component is exhausted.
example: Breadth-first search uses a queue; depth-first search follows an unfinished branch before returning to alternatives.
confusion: Visiting one start vertex’s reachable component does not necessarily visit every vertex of the graph.

name: Discovery and marking
quick: Recording that a vertex has been encountered for the first time.
definition: To discover a vertex is to encounter it for the first time during a traversal. Marking records that fact, often with a true-or-false flag. Discovery order lists first encounters only, even when a route later revisits a vertex.
example: If a traversal first sees $a,b,d$, then later returns to $b$, the discovery list still begins $a,b,d$.
confusion: A sequence of first discoveries need not itself be a walk: consecutive discoveries can lie on different branches.

name: Backtracking
quick: Returning to an earlier unfinished choice after a branch is exhausted.
definition: During depth-first search, when a vertex has no unvisited neighbor left to explore, return to the earlier vertex that led to it. Continue until an unfinished branch is found or the search is complete. A stack or recursive calls keep track of this return information.
example: After exploring leaf $d$ from $b$, return to $b$ before trying another child of $b$.
confusion: Returning along a search route is not a new discovery of a previously visited vertex.

name: Weighted graph
quick: A graph with a numerical value assigned to each edge.
definition: An edge weight represents a quantity such as distance, travel time, or cost. For a weighted route, its total weight is the sum of its edge weights. An unweighted graph treats every edge alike when counting route length.
example: A two-edge route with weights 1 and 1 costs 2, less than a one-edge route of weight 10.
confusion: Breadth-first search minimizes the number of edges in an unweighted graph; it does not generally minimize arbitrary total weight.

name: Complete graph
quick: A simple undirected graph with an edge between every pair of distinct vertices.
definition: A complete graph includes every possible connection between distinct vertices, with no loops or repeated edges. With n vertices, every vertex has degree n-1 and there are n(n-1)/2 edges.
example: The complete graph on four vertices has six edges and every degree is 3.
confusion: “Complete” does not mean that an arbitrary drawing has been finished; it specifies a precise connection pattern.

name: Algorithm
quick: A specified procedure for carrying out a task.
definition: An algorithm states repeatable steps for obtaining an output or performing a task from the allowed inputs. Mathematical analysis distinguishes whether the procedure gives the right result, whether it terminates, and how much work it uses.
example: To add a finite list of numbers, start a running total at zero, add each listed number to it in turn, and return the total after the last number.
confusion: A description of a desired result is not yet a procedure for obtaining it.

name: Direct indexing
quick: Accessing an array entry using its position.
definition: An array representation stores entries so that their numerical positions identify where to access them. Under the stated unit-cost model, reading one valid indexed entry counts as a constant amount of work, independent of the total array size.
example: If vertices are numbered, the adjacency-matrix entry in row 2 and column 5 answers one adjacency query.
confusion: Finding a label’s index can require extra work if no direct label-to-index mapping has been supplied.

name: Bit-operation model
quick: A cost model that counts work on individual binary digits.
definition: A bit-operation model measures work in operations on binary digits. Arithmetic on long integers then costs more than arithmetic on short integers, so an operation count that treats every large-integer arithmetic step as one unit may change.
example: Adding two positive integers represented by b binary digits can require processing all b digit positions.
confusion: An integer’s numerical magnitude and the number of bits representing it are different measures of input size.
